The bursting phenomenon in neurons is a widespread occurrence that remains poorly understood. This study explores the role of short-term synaptic plasticity in generating bursts, focusing on a simple network of two neurons with a LTP mechanism based on the spike pair stimulus. We found that this model can replicate the basic features of bursting, including sensitivity to specific stimulus patterns and the separation of time between consecutive bursts. This research contributes to the development of a comprehensive theory of bursting, which can be applied to various types of neuronal networks.

The concept of the Wu-Yang flux tube is examined in the context of a spin-1/2 planar rotor in a magnetic field.  It is shown that the WY flux tube leads to the emergence of a topologically protected edge mode, which exhibits chiral behavior.

We investigate the average number of times a Brownian particle collides with a moving wall within a cavity over a prolonged period. It is found that the average number of collisions is directly related to the logarithm of time. This is further explored in the context of a cell with constantly shifting boundaries, where the average number of collisions is linked to the cell volume and the rate of boundary movement scaled by the squared diffusion coefficient and the square root of time.
We categorize the finite group of mapping class groups for certain types of hyperbolic L-space knots, showing that any such group can be represented by at most five elements.

This study establishes a connection between kinetic theory and macroscopic fluid dynamics by deriving the compressible Euler equations from a kinetic theory framework. We begin by modeling a system of weakly inelastic particles whose interactions are governed by a hard-sphere potential and whose phase space is described by a Boltzmann collision kernel. Assuming these particles are randomly dispersed and that their velocity distribution function decays exponentially for increasing velocity, we obtain an explicit solution for the Boltzmann equation and subsequently obtain its hydrodynamic limit through a mathematical technique that involves truncating velocity space. This technique, which is analogous to the Hilbert expansion, allows us to prove the convergence of the velocity distribution function to an Eulerian scalar field representing the local particle density.

The growing number of available detectors has led to a shift in focus from individual models to ensemble learning for real-world applications. However, current approaches often treat each model independently, failing to leverage the unique strengths of each one. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework that allows for the real-time combination of multiple detectors, eliminating the need for additional data preprocessing. By utilizing a modified version of the Viterbi algorithm, our approach efficiently handles algorithmic complexity while providing improved performance. Our results demonstrate that this framework can enhance the performance of individual models and reveal their strengths through the use of a new model signature space.

Research has extensively examined how code elements are named, but the impact of naming patterns on code readability and understanding remains unclear. To address this gap, we conducted a study to investigate how identifier naming affects developers' comprehension of code. In our experiment, participants were asked to review code and predict how it would function, with code snippets either following a naming convention related to its purpose or focusing on its data type. Our results showed that developers who interact more frequently with code perform significantly better on the purpose-based naming tasks, but are hindered by the data-type based naming tasks. These findings suggest that developers' comprehension of code is influenced by the naming patterns used, with implications for how identifier naming should be approached.

We demonstrate that a specific free $\mathcal{O}_q$-module, denoted as $M_{(n)}$, is irreducible and has a dimension of $n+1$. Furthermore, we prove that $M_{(1)}$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal{O}_q$ and that it has a unique nilpotent element. We also establish that for any $n$, the module $M_{(n)}$ can be expressed as the quotient of two modules, $M_{(n+1)}$ divided by $M_{(n)}$, where $M_{(n)}$ is a submodule of $M_{(n+1)}$.

A statistical model of grain growth in two-phase systems has been developed, 
accounting for grain size distribution and polycrystalline microstructure. 
This model is based on a stochastic cluster-cluster aggregation model, 
where the formation of new grains occurs through the coalescence of major-phase 
grains, while the minor phase serves as a barrier inhibiting grain growth. 
Numerical simulations of the grain-size distribution were performed, 
revealing a significant impact of the minor phase on grain growth. 
It was found that the growth rate is primarily influenced by the volume 
fraction of the major phase, while the grain size distribution is affected 
by both volume and interface fractions of the minor phase. 
This model can be applied to various multiphase systems, 
enabling predictions of the grain-size distribution and microstructure evolution 
under different conditions, such as varying volume fractions or grain sizes.

This study presents a comprehensive evaluation of the most recent human mesh recovery methods, utilizing publicly available datasets. Our research reveals that selecting the right dataset features and configuring the hyperparameters significantly influences the performance of these methods. To address this challenge, we introduce a simple yet effective approach called Mesh Recoverer Finder (MRF), which automatically optimizes the hyperparameters and dataset features to achieve the best results. Our MRF method is then applied to four human mesh recovery methods and demonstrated to enhance their performance. Furthermore, we provide a thorough analysis of the strengths and limitations of these methods, aiming to facilitate the development of new research in this field.

In this research, we have calculated the superconducting transition temperature Tc and the critical magnetic field Hc for an electron gas with an effective mass ratio of m_e/m_* equal to 0.02, 0.05, and 0.10. The calculations were performed for different strengths of the electron correlation parameter U, ranging from 0.5 to 10 times the electron-electron hybridization energy. Our results show that the superconducting transition temperature Tc and the critical magnetic field Hc decrease as the strength of electron attraction increases. The superconducting transition temperature Tc and the critical magnetic field Hc are also found to be affected by the electron-electron hybridization energy U, with Tc and Hc decreasing as U increases.

A comprehensive matching of the Standard Model to an effective field theory up to leading order in dimensional-6 operators has been achieved for the process of Higgs decay into a W+ W- pair in the electroweak theory at one-loop order. The resulting matching conditions were derived using a detailed analysis of the ultraviolet divergences in dimensional regularization, yielding a set of matching conditions that are consistent with previous findings at tree level. The findings are expected to provide valuable insights for precision Higgs physics studies.

This paper provides a conceptual overview of the field of machine learning and surveys recent advancements in the field. We focus on key aspects such as gradient-based machine learning, statistical machine learning, and ensemble learning, also highlighting the role of big data and the growing importance of the Internet of Things (IoT). While the paper does not aim to be an exhaustive review, we do explore the potential of machine learning to address critical challenges in the field of energy management. We also discuss the key challenges and future research opportunities within this domain.

This study introduces an innovative, optimal terminal sliding mode control strategy to minimize total error at the end of settling time in second-order uncertain systems. By transforming the optimal switching problem into a dynamic programming problem, an optimal switching sequence is determined, then converted into a state-dependent Riccati equation to design a robust terminal sliding mode controller. The proposed control scheme's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulation comparisons.

The quality control of lithium-ion batteries can significantly benefit from
ultrasound resonance technology. By analyzing the resonant frequency of an
ultrasonic transducer embedded within a fully assembled battery, it is possible
to assess the internal state of the battery. This research explores the
relationship between the measured resonant frequencies and physical properties
of lithium-ion batteries. We employed a non-contact measurement technique to
determine the resonant frequency of batteries in various states of aging. The
results show that the measured frequencies are highly correlated with the
battery's age, weight, capacity, and state of health.

This paper presents a novel approach to designing flatness-based controllers for discrete-time nonlinear systems. Unlike the conventional method of applying continuous-time flatness properties to systems of continuity, this approach specifically addresses discrete-time systems. In order to achieve this, we first develop flatness-based controller design methods for discrete-time systems. Our analysis reveals that the discrete-time flat output sequence yields a specific structure, which is distinct from its continuous-time counterpart. Consequently, we propose a novel method to design flatness-based controllers for discrete-time systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the existing flatness-based controller design method for discrete-time systems is a special case of our newly developed approach.

Our research focuses on enhancing the accuracy of image descriptions produced by artificial intelligence models. We suggest combining pre-annotated datasets with extensive datasets obtained from the web, like image search results. This approach enables us to leverage web-scale data without the need for manual annotation. To achieve this, we employ a multi-stage framework that includes a method to identify relevant web images, generate descriptive text, and correct any inaccuracies in the generated descriptions. Our method utilizes a curated dataset to establish a baseline and refine descriptions produced by a language model. Our experimental findings indicate that this technique produces more accurate image descriptions than existing methods, both quantitatively and qualitatively.

We investigate the relationship between the maximum number of strings of a fixed length that map to a particular set of strings, containing at least a specified percentage of strings that have a consistent pattern. This relationship is studied within the context of a bipartite graph where the strings are represented as vertices and edge connections indicate pattern consistency. A lower bound is established on the number of strings that can be in the set, given the percentage of strings with a consistent pattern. This lower bound is demonstrated to be within a constant factor of an upper bound when the set of strings is considered.

We identify restricted version semigroups within the ordered Ehresmann semigroup framework. Furthermore, we establish that these semigroups are equivalent to a specific class of partial row inverse semigroups. Additionally, we classify one and two-sided restriction semigroups as the respective left and right E-semigroups. To this end, we have a comprehensive description of one and two-sided restriction semigroups. These descriptions encompass the semigroups that possess a specific type of regularity, as well as those that possess a specific type of regular left and right E-semigroup structure. Finally, we have a detailed description of two-sided restriction semigroups.

The self-attention mechanism has been a driving force in the current state of NLP advancements, with a wide range of applications across various tasks. Despite its impressive capabilities, a recent study found that a 1-Trillion parameter self-attention model achieved the optimal performance with a specific layer width of 512. This paper delves into the theoretical underpinnings of self-attention, providing a comprehensive analysis of its theoretical properties. We establish a connection between the model's performance and its capacity for generalization, with a specific focus on its ability to learn complex functions. Our research also uncovers an optimal layer width for the model, which aligns with its optimal performance at 1-Trillion parameters. This discovery is a significant breakthrough, offering a theoretical explanation for the optimal performance of self-attention models.

BIO$_{3}$ nanoparticles have been studied extensively for their potential in solar energy conversion due to their ability to exhibit multiferroic properties at room temperature. However, the efficiency of solar energy conversion in these nanoparticles is hindered by their bandgap, which is significantly lower than the energy threshold required for efficient conversion. Our research has found that BIO$_{3}$ nanoparticles possess a unique bandgap structure, characterized by a localized state, which is a result of the nanoparticles' high surface-to-volume ratio. This unique bandgap structure has been confirmed by theoretical calculations and experimental analysis. Our findings suggest that the localized state in these nanoparticles acts as a barrier to charge separation, which is a critical requirement for solar energy conversion. These results have significant implications for the development of solar energy conversion devices using BIO$_{3}$ nanoparticles.

A detailed examination of the extended $331$ symmetry model is presented, with a specific focus on the mass-generation processes for the bottom quark and tau lepton. Building on the initial mass-generation for the top quark via the $t\bar{t}$ process, we consider the interaction between the top quark and a heavy $Z'$ boson, which then decays into a tau lepton and a massless neutrino, and also decay into a massless neutrino and bottom quark. We also investigate the mass-generation for the bottom quark and tau lepton through the interaction with a $Z$ boson, which is a mixture of a $Z$ and $Z'$ boson. We then calculate the mass of the bottom quark and tau lepton in terms of the mass of the top quark and other model parameters. We also derive the mass of the tau lepton in terms of the mass of the bottom quark.

This research paper introduces a groundbreaking approach to learning the physical characteristics of common, hand-held items. Our novel architecture leverages a signed distance field and an implicit network to create a precise three-dimensional representation of these objects, enabling us to recover their shapes from a single RGB image. Our method excels in both visual and practical applications, as it can be employed in conjunction with a robotic arm to manipulate unfamiliar objects. Our results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods, both visually and in terms of accuracy, as demonstrated through quantitative metrics.

The study of the Sun's outer layers has been a primary focus of the GOLF instrument on SOHO for over two decades. The GOLF team has recently completed a major phase of data collection, having obtained 28000 continuous, nearly daily spectra from the instrument. The GOLF team has developed an innovative method for analyzing the data, known as Equal Contrast, which leverages the instrument's angular contrast to examine variations in the Sun's chromosphere. The new technique is expected to provide valuable insights into the dynamics of the Sun's outer layers over the long-term dataset collected by GOLF.

The LHCb experiment has conducted a search for the leptonically decaying process $\Sigma^+ \to e^+ e^-\gamma$, where the decay proceeds via the emission of a virtual $W$ boson from a virtual $J/\psi$ or $J/\psi^{(\prime)}$. No evidence was found for the associated background process $\Sigma^+ \to p e^+ e^-\gamma$, and a 90% confidence upper limit was established for the branching ratio of $\Sigma^+ \to e^+ e^-\gamma$, specifically $2.9 \times 10^{-6}$. The analysis utilized a dataset of $3.0$ fb$^{-1}$ proton-proton collision events, recorded at a centre-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 7$ TeV, utilizing the LHCb detector.

In parallel symbolic execution, the domain-specific code is modified with pseudocode to efficiently identify vulnerabilities. A flexible approach to this process involves dividing tasks between workers based on their ability to process different parts of the code. To optimize this method, we've developed a new system that breaks down the evaluation process into smaller components and allows for various strategies to be employed. Our results show that a straightforward technique can be effective in distributing tasks and that using it with a particular method yields better results than other approaches.

The decay of magnetization in anisotropic magnetic nanoparticles is studied under the influence of thermal fluctuations and Brownian rotation.  A probabilistic model is developed to describe the random orientation changes caused by these factors.  A solution to the resulting master equation is obtained analytically for various initial conditions and compared with numerical simulations.  The results show that the rate of magnetization decay is directly proportional to the angle between the direction of anisotropy and the direction of an applied magnetic field.  This discovery leads to a method for adjusting the angle of anisotropy to control the decay rate, thereby enhancing the performance of magnetic sensors and motors.

Federated learning enables training on decentralized data while preserving client privacy, but its efficiency is hindered by communication constraints. A novel online algorithm, Online Push-Sum (OPS), has been proposed to address these limitations by enabling local gradient aggregation without a central server. Through clever data packaging and transmission, OPS achieves efficient communication, but its performance is not without its drawbacks. A recent study has demonstrated that OPS is susceptible to malicious data manipulation by adversarial clients, which can compromise model training. However, researchers have devised a secure framework to mitigate these attacks, incorporating a robust verification mechanism to safeguard against malicious data injection. By validating the effectiveness of this approach, researchers have achieved a significant 20% improvement in model training stability and a 40% reduction in communication costs.

Predicting dialog acts is a crucial component in understanding conversational behavior.
While current models have shown significant progress, they primarily focus on individual turn-level information and often overlook preceding short texts that may contain essential contextual details.
To address this limitation, we propose incorporating multi-granularity information through a network that integrates preceding short texts at the word and dialogue levels.
Our experiments demonstrate that considering these multiple scales of preceding short texts leads to improved dialog act prediction performance.

We have developed a comprehensive model for etalon-based instruments, both collimated and telecentric, to predict their performance and optical quality. This model is based on a rigorous, analytical framework that accounts for etalon surface figure, including both symmetry and asymmetry, to calculate the optical transfer function. The model's predictions align with the results of extensive laboratory tests, demonstrating its effectiveness in simulating real-world scenarios. Our analysis highlights the impact of instrument design choices on performance, particularly with regard to etalon symmetry, which our model shows to be less critical for telecentric instruments.

A set of points in the plane is considered "labelled" if each point has a unique label assigned to it, and there exists a set of lines connecting these points, such that for every line, the points at either end share the same label.  A subset of points A forms a "partial labelling" if each point in A has a unique label assigned to it.  The size of the smallest set of points required to form a partial labelling that allows a compatible matching to consist of only one edge, is denoted by f(n).  It has been previously established that f(n) is at most 2n-1.  We prove that f(n) is at least n/2 + 1, and in fact, we show that any set of n points that allows a compatible matching to consist of only one edge, must have at least (n/2 + 1) copies of a specific subset of points.  This result is obtained by showing that for any partial labelling, the points that do not participate in the matching, form a region bounded by lines that connect the points of the matching, and that these lines intersect in a specific pattern.  This result has implications for the minimum number of lines required to enclose a specific region of points, and we show that this number is at least (n^2/4), and we provide a construction to show that this lower bound is tight.

In this research, we introduce Codelet, a proposed execution model for large-scale chiplet-based systems. Codelet represents a compact, lightweight code segment that serves as the core computational unit within a code domain. Code domains are categorized into three types: data domains, interface domains, and fabric domains, each containing their respective Codelet cores. Codelets are mapped to fabric domains, where they execute within a fabric's processing grid, utilizing a network of interfaces to interact with surrounding code domains. Codelets are also capable of being replicated to enhance performance, thereby facilitating efficient execution of complex tasks. To demonstrate the viability of Codelet, we have developed a comprehensive software stack, including a compiler, runtime, and synthetic applications, and have successfully executed it on a cutting-edge chiplet system.

In survival analysis, the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator is sensitive to the distribution of the data, which can lead to poor estimation results. To mitigate this issue, researchers have proposed a data transformation method called presmoothing, which helps stabilize the fitting process. Although presmoothing has been shown to improve the stability of maximum likelihood estimation, its effects on other estimation methods are not well understood. To address this knowledge gap, we have conducted a comprehensive study comparing presmoothing with alternative estimation approaches, including the empirical transformation estimator and the Breslow estimator. Our findings suggest that presmoothing consistently yields more accurate results than maximum likelihood estimation, particularly in scenarios with high censoring rates. In contrast, presmoothing was found to be less effective than the empirical transformation estimator in terms of mean squared error, although it demonstrated greater robustness to data irregularities. Furthermore, our investigation revealed that presmoothing can outperform the Breslow estimator in terms of mean squared error, especially when the hazard rates are constant or increasing monotonically.

The nonlocal metric dimension of a graph G is defined as the smallest number of nodes needed to determine the neighborhood of every node. In this study, we explore the nonlocal metric dimension of various graph classes and provide specific characterizations for several families of graphs. We find that 1-neighborly graphs and a specific subset of Cayley graphs have either a 1-dimensional or (n-2) dimensional nonlocal metric dimension. Furthermore, we establish that 1-vertex-connected, noncomplete bipartite graphs have a 2-dimensional or (n-1) dimensional nonlocal metric dimension. In addition, we demonstrate that 1-vertex-connected, noncomplete bipartite Cayley graphs have a 1-dimensional, 2-dimensional, or (n-1) dimensional nonlocal metric dimension. We also show that 1-neighborly Cayley graphs have a 1-dimensional or (n-2) dimensional nonlocal metric dimension.

This paper introduces a side-channel attack strategy targeting the PNN architecture by analyzing power traces. The attack strategy leverages a deep learning approach to efficiently determine the internal state of the PNN at various stages. The proposed method is implemented in two versions: one utilizing a deep learning network to estimate intermediate states, and the other employing a generative model to predict the internal state of the PNN. The experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a high success rate of over 90% on a well-secured system, and it also outperforms a previously developed method for state estimation.

This research introduces a novel method to minimize polarization responses in linear and nonlinear systems by utilizing bounds on partial distances. The approach involves setting a lower and upper limit on the partial distances, then constructing an optimal sequence of states that spans the signal space, achieving the estimated minimum polarization after each step within the bounds. The method is based on a set of inequalities derived from the Cramer-Rao inequalities, which provide necessary conditions for the partial distances. The method is illustrated with examples from optimal detection problems, where the optimal sequence of states and the corresponding minimum polarization are determined for both coherent and adaptive sequences.

A novel approach to self-supervised denoising in seismic data processing has been developed, which leverages initial supervised training on synthetic datasets to enhance denoising performance in complex field data. This method demonstrates the potential for unsupervised denoising in real data by using the pre-trained network to correct issues like convolutional filter instability and signal loss during the denoising process. Furthermore, an adaptive masking strategy is implemented to preserve essential signals while eliminating noisy artifacts. This technique has shown promising results in denoising data from various sources, including land, transition, and oceanic environments.

In our study, we investigate the real photon emission effect on the charge asymmetry in lepton-proton scattering within the context of one-boson exchange framework. We have derived the formulae for the charge asymmetry in lepton-proton scattering in the one-photon and one-pion exchange mechanisms, taking into account real photon emission. Utilizing these formulas, we have calculated the charge asymmetry in muon-proton scattering with emitted photons and found that the real photon effect has a considerable impact on the charge asymmetry.

Theoretical research on the electronic structure of Mott insulators with doped holes has been conducted, focusing on the impact of spin-polaronic spectra on hole dynamics. Our study demonstrates that the presence of spin-polaronic spectra influences the electronic structure of Mott insulators in anisotropic systems, such as triangular and square lattice antiferromagnets. Specifically, we found that the spin-polaronic spectra in these systems are characterized by ladder structures, resulting in a suppression of doped holes' phase space and a suppression of doped holes' phase space and a suppression of their mobility. Furthermore, we found that the spin-polaronic spectra in these systems are characterized by ladder structures, resulting in a suppression of doped holes' phase space and a suppression of their mobility. Our study also reveals that the spin-polaronic spectra in these systems are characterized by ladder structures, resulting in a suppression of doped holes' phase space and a suppression of their mobility.

This research develops a novel estimation approach for causal analysis of ongoing treatments, which retains key performance guarantees in the face of treatment interference. By combining established double machine learning strategies with a recent method for analyzing average treatment effects in interdependent situations, the approach offers a robust framework for analyzing continuous interventions. Through a study of this strategy, the advantages of continuous treatment estimation over traditional methods are clarified, particularly in situations involving high-dimensional covariates. Empirical data from simulated and real-world studies confirm the effectiveness of this strategy.

Recent research into starshades has gained momentum, prompting a call for 
a new conference on the topic to leverage recent breakthroughs and 
unite recent studies, thereby fueling future scientific inquiry. This 
call-to-action is bolstered by an upcoming conference, NSF-NATP's 2022 
Starshades Conference, which will bring together recent research and 
welcome contributions from both established and emerging areas. This 
contribution outlines the rationale for an updated starshades conference, 
identifies potential gaps in current research, and proposes an 
aggressive new agenda for starshades studies.

The recent Suicidal Ideation Questionnaire (SIQ) dataset by Li et al. is a pioneering effort in using natural language processing to identify suicidal texts online. Building upon this innovation, we introduce the Robin dataset, which surpasses the SIQ dataset in several key aspects. Our Robin dataset comprises 2,000 text samples, each annotated with five points on a spectrum by human experts, and it outperforms the SIQ dataset in terms of size, diversity of domains, and annotation precision. We also develop and evaluate a range of models that effectively leverage the Robin dataset's unique annotation structure.

A novel approach to constructing a five-parameter supersymmetric action is introduced, which leverages the principles of Bootstrapping and the AdS/CFT correspondence. Employing a combination of superfields and the Capelli-Dashkevich operator, a free theory is constructed, which can be precisely solved using the bootstrap method. This yields a constraint on the super-Schwarzians, which can be mapped to a specific equation involving the AdS 5 supermetric. This constraint can be precisely solved using the AdS/CFT correspondence and yields a corresponding field theory in flat space. This method can be applied to construct actions with higher parameters and suggests the possibility of a general solution.

This research explores the concept of conjugacy between two rational dynamical systems, examining its implications for the dynamics of a difference equation. By establishing a link between conjugacy and the equation's fixed points, we identify a specific condition under which two systems are conjugate. Our results have significant applications in the fields of biology, medicine, and statistics, particularly in understanding population growth patterns. Furthermore, our findings provide insight into the behavior of rational maps, with implications for the study of chaotic dynamics.

This paper explores a family of electrically charged black holes in anti-de Sitter space, where a specific field equation is used to describe a system with both general relativity and nonlinear electrodynamics. The analysis reveals that the solution space includes a family of static black holes in both four and five dimensions. The analysis further examines the properties of these black holes, including their behavior at different temperatures and torques, and determines the critical values associated with thermodynamic transitions. The results also include solutions for black holes with both positive and negative charges in the context of a system with a specific type of matter that is coupled to gravity. The analysis further examines the properties of these black holes in the context of a system with a specific type of matter that is coupled to gravity and determines the critical values associated with thermodynamic transitions.

We consider a non-zero integer vector $\mathbf{c}$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and a positive real $\delta$ less than one, and we define $\mathbf{c}$-Sidon sets $\mathrm{Sid}(\mathbf{c})$. We prove that for any integer $N$ greater than or equal to one, and any integer $d$ greater than or below $N/(\log N)^{\delta}$, we can find a subset $A$ of the set of integers $\{1, 2, \ldots, N\}^d$ that is Sidon for $\mathbf{c}$ and has cardinality $N^{\frac{d}{2} - \frac{1}{36} + o(1)}$. This generalizes a previous result of Bourgain and the author, and improves the exponent $\frac{d}{2} - \frac{1}{12} - \frac{1}{60}$ found in that paper. We prove that for any integer $d$ greater than or equal to two, and any integer $N$ greater than or below $N^{1/d} (\log N)^{d}$, we can find a subset $A$ of the set of integers $\{1, 2, \ldots, N\}^d$ that is Sidon for $\mathbf{c}$ and has cardinality $N^{\frac

A geometric phase is demonstrated to emerge in a spin-1/2 system on a triangular lattice, subject to external magnetic fields that induce quantum phase transitions. These transitions occur when the ground-state structure within the system changes, specifically from a N\'{e}el to a stripy configuration and then to a three-fold ring arrangement. The magnetic susceptibility at these transitions is found to correlate directly with the geometric phase, which increases as the system approaches the critical point, making it possible to monitor these phase changes via susceptibility measurements.

The behavior of ferromagnetic systems can be significantly influenced by critical fluctuations that emerge during a relaxation process from high temperatures to the Curie temperature. This study explores the impact of these fluctuations on the mean-field spin system, which exhibits a spontaneous magnetization reversal. By incorporating the effects of critical fluctuations, our analysis reveals that the spin system's behavior is characterized by a power-law distribution of waiting times. This power-law distribution is found to be controlled by a scaling exponent that is inversely proportional to the critical exponent of the magnetization. Our findings provide new insights into the role of critical fluctuations in shaping the spin system's behavior, which can be applied to the study of relaxation processes in various magnetic systems.

The transition from localization to delocalization in quasicrystals is largely influenced by the way the states in different energy ranges interact across the spectrum. In this study, we investigate this phenomenon through the lens of a random matrix model, which reveals that the critical behavior of these systems is characterized by the way the states in different energy ranges become correlated. By analyzing the model, we identify a critical point that marks the onset of this correlation and show that it is associated with a shift in the universality class of these systems.

Task-oriented dialogue systems in multiple languages rely on extensive annotated datasets to learn. These datasets are typically compiled from existing dialogues, transcribed, and annotated either manually or through automated processes. The challenge lies in obtaining a substantial multilingual corpus, as it often involves costly and time-consuming human annotation. To overcome this hurdle, we explore the feasibility of leveraging machine translation to generate multilingual dialogues. By utilizing a cross-lingual dialogue generation model, we can produce dialogues in one language and have them translated into another, thereby facilitating multilingual task-oriented dialogue. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through experiments on a Spanish-English dataset, where we successfully generate multilingual dialogues and demonstrate the potential of this method.

RNA-seq time series data analysis is crucial in understanding disease progression and response to treatment. Our research presents DiffSplicing, a novel R package capable of analyzing RNA-seq time series data using a generalized linear model and multivariate Bayesian testing for differential expression and splicing. Additionally, DiffSplicing offers a unique gene plot view that visualizes gene expression changes over time, along with the level of significance. This package also facilitates the identification of genes exhibiting delayed or accelerated changes in expression.

To protect data, technical measures are widely adopted to safeguard individual information. However, the implementation of these measures often involves lengthy negotiations between legal and engineering teams, which can lead to significant delays in data protection. To address this challenge, our research aims to develop a system that automatically creates technical measures based on legal requirements. Our initial step involves analyzing the current state of technical measures, which are often poorly defined and lack clear guidelines. We then identify the common challenges faced by legal and engineering teams during implementation. Based on this understanding, we propose a concept for automated technical measure creation and demonstrate its feasibility through a practical example.

In the context of the Color Glass Condensate formalism, we investigate correlations between particles produced in the early stages of heavy ion collisions, specifically focusing on the azimuthal correlations of four or more particles. Our calculations involve a nonlinear equation for the azimuthal correlations and show that they can be accurately described by a specific method, yielding results consistent with both experimental findings and theoretical predictions. Notably, our work reveals distinct patterns in the correlations, such as a 'diamond' shape, which can be attributed to nonlinear effects. These findings have significant implications for LHC and RHIC experiments, where similar correlations are expected to occur.

This research examines how the production of light nuclei such as deuterons, helium, and tritons is affected by coalescence in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. The study utilizes the AMPT model to simulate the collision and analyze the data, finding that the AMPT model accurately reproduces the yields of these nuclei but not their transverse momentum spectra. The model reveals that the production of these nuclei is influenced by various factors including the coalescence from higher-order sources, the transverse momentum of particles involved, and the correlation between the momenta of particles involved in coalescence. The study also shows that the transverse momentum spectra of these nuclei can be explained by the transition from a Bose-Einstein statistical regime to a Fermi-like regime at a certain level of transverse momentum.

The discovery of numerous rocky exoplanets with potential for hosting life has revealed a vastly different picture of life-supporting atmospheres on these planets than we previously imagined. The diversity of atmospheric compositions on these exoplanets is significantly higher than expected, and this is largely due to the complex interactions between the planet's atmosphere, interior, and the radiation it receives from its star. This article provides an overview of the various factors contributing to the diversity of atmospheric compositions on exoplanets and discusses the challenges associated with observing these effects. The review also explores the implications of these factors for the search for extraterrestrial life and the importance of integrating data from multiple observations, such as those from the James Webb Space Telescope, transit spectroscopy, and planetary interior studies.

Circulant graphs are a specific type of graph that can be described as r-circulant graphs when jump lengths of their vertices reach r values.  If r is 0 or greater than 3, the graph's degree of dispersability is known;  However, for 0<r<3, the graph's degree of dispersability is still uncertain.  This paper focuses on the r=1 case, examining the dispersability of 1-regular graphs, which are also known as cycles.  It's discovered that a cycle of n length is dispersable if n is 1, 2, or 5.  If n is 3, 4, or 6, the cycle is dispersable if it can be divided by the jump length r, with r being 2.  If n is 3, 4, or 6, the cycle is dispersable if it can be divided by the jump length r, with r being 2.  If n is 7 or greater, the cycle is dispersable if it can be divided by the jump length r, with r being 2. This paper explores the nested Neumann algorithm within the context of regularized optimization, particularly for smooth and strongly convex objectives. By applying the Neumann algorithm to the dual problem, and employing nested iterations, researchers have achieved a novel solution to the primal problem via its KKT dual counterpart. Our research aims to extend this approach to address the convergence of second-order stochastic nested Neumann algorithm for large-scale problems. We establish a convergence rate for this algorithm, contingent upon the depth of inception depth, thereby enhancing existing knowledge on nested Neumann algorithm. Our theoretical findings are substantiated through numerical experiments.

The impact of cosmic friction on the curvature of matter perturbations during the inflationary epoch is investigated. It is discovered that the friction term boosts the curvature of perturbations in a single-field inflationary model, yet diminishes the boost in a multi-field model where the evolution of the field is influenced by cosmic friction. Furthermore, the theoretical framework of the single-field case is extended to the non-attractor regime, where it's observed that the boost effect is notably reduced.

In the context of revenue management, we develop a model that accounts for a significant issue - the negative impact of offering discounted fares on the airline's overall sales. To address this, we introduce a novel approach centered around a key decision-making point: when to stop offering discounted fares to a customer, who is currently considering a purchase. This decision is influenced by the probability of the customer making a purchase at the current price, and the potential loss from inducing demand and not capturing it. Our model is based on a mathematical function representing the airline's optimal strategy, which we analyze and apply in two scenarios: a simplified model and a more realistic simulation that mimics a real-world situation. The results of our simulation demonstrate that our approach outperforms a traditional method, and that offering limited fares can actually boost sales.

The casebase package in R offers a comprehensive framework for analyzing data on survival times by integrating various techniques, including regression, stratification, and prediction, within a unified approach. This package builds upon existing methods, providing a more flexible and efficient platform for users to conduct complex analyses. Key features of casebase include support for multiple models, stratified analysis, prediction, and confidence interval calculations, all designed to enhance statistical precision. This package is particularly useful when working with data from clinical trials, providing users with a range of statistical tools. This documentation serves as a reference guide for the casebase package, covering its key functions and features.

A novel semi-numeric approach is developed to solve the Schrodinger equation, achieving greater accuracy through the use of an average potential and iterative corrections, thereby reducing the computational cost. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through the application to three particles (pion, proton, and neutron) with the Booznyuk-Promskiy potential, resulting in a more precise determination of masses than the average potential model. The improvement in accuracy is notable, particularly in calculating total wave functions, scattering lengths, and binding energies. The method's potential for further applications in particle physics is also explored.

Traditional file systems built on the POSIX standard, such as those used in research centers, are designed to handle the needs of individual users and small groups, but struggle with scalability issues when dealing with large numbers of users. In contrast, cloud storage platforms, such as HDFS, are designed to handle massive amounts of data from a high volume of users, but are often restrictive and don't provide the level of control that researchers need. This paper proposes a new cloud storage system, OSCAR, that combines the scalability of HDFS with the control and features of traditional file systems. OSCAR is built using an object storage model, but also includes object-based file systems, such as OSCARFS, that provide additional features. OSCARFS is designed to handle high levels of metadata and file system traffic, and provides a stable and performant environment for researchers. OSCAR is tested on a large-scale HPC system, and the results show that it can handle the needs of large research groups while providing a high degree of control and performance.

The widespread adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) has led to a significant increase in demand for charging facilities, particularly in urban areas. However, the scarcity of limited charging resources has resulted in a first-come-first-served allocation, causing EVs to wait for extended periods. To mitigate this issue, we propose an online pricing mechanism that optimizes charging resource allocation in a dynamic parking lot. Our approach involves developing a series of algorithms that operate without prior knowledge of future demand or arrival patterns and are designed to maximize the revenue generated from selling charging resources. We establish theoretical performance bounds for these algorithms and demonstrate their effectiveness through simulations, which show that they outperform a baseline approach in terms of revenue and charging resource allocation.

This paper proposes novel creation techniques for complex Hermitian (L, Q)-codes through the extension of existing Hermitian (L, Q)-codes. The paper outlines the development of new Hermitian LCD codes with longer lengths by modifying existing codes. The constructed codes possess the property of being locally indistinguishable from one another. The proposed creation methods are applicable to both non-quotient (L, Q)-codes and those with a quotient structure.

Researchers have made significant progress in computing the $ℏ^{-4}$-order scattering amplitude for black holes in Einstein gravity combined with a single scalar field, a previously uncomputed amplitude. The study has yielded numerical results for the scattering of black holes with equal mass and identical sizes across a range of scattering angles. Building upon this work, our research extends previous findings by computing the $ℰ^{(6)}_g$ and $\mathcal{M}^{(6)}_\phi$ integrals up to a specific order of integration by parts integration. These results were obtained using the UV/IR duality of string theory applied to a specific worldsheet scalar theory. The study has provided numerical results for the resulting scattering amplitude across a range of angles and sizes.

The integration of variable renewable energy sources into the power grid has led to increased land requirements for solar and wind installations, which in turn raises concerns about land use and its associated costs. While some argue that these costs can be substantial, the actual impact on electricity pricing remains unclear. This study examines the potential land-related expenses associated with expanding solar and wind site capacities in the German power grid, and their influence on future electricity prices. By employing a comprehensive power grid simulation model, we simulate various scenarios representing the development of solar and wind sites, and then analyze the resulting effects on electricity prices. Our findings indicate that increased land use for solar and wind sites leads to higher electricity prices, with the risk of land acquisition becoming a significant obstacle to achieving ambitious clean energy goals, particularly if the expansion of solar sites continues unabated.

Cluster-randomized trials frequently employ marginal analysis, which focuses on the direct impact of treatment. However, this approach is estimable only when the average cluster size remains constant, and this is not commonly the case in studies involving family-based sampling. We propose a novel method for estimating the direct treatment effect using a conditional approach, where clusters are treated as a group. This method is applied in a study examining the effectiveness of an adolescent family-centered HIV prevention program.

This paper delves into the topological properties of a specific category of networks characterized by the absence of loops and self-links. These networks comprise nodes that can be either passive or active. The nodes are interconnected through a specific set of edges defined by two distinct rules. The first rule states that two active nodes can be directly connected to each other. The second rule specifies that an active node can be linked to two passive nodes. The focus of this research is to derive mathematical expressions for various topological indices, such as the multiplicative degree-Kirchhoff index, Wiener index, and Szeged index, in terms of network parameters. The derived expressions are then used to investigate the asymptotic behavior of these indices as the network size increases.

We investigate contextual linear bandits where the goal is to optimize reward functions that depend on hidden parameters in a known class. Our focus is on how the context distribution affects communication complexity, which measures the minimal number of bits needed to convey parameter values. In contextual linear bandits, the context distribution influences the required communication bits, as it determines the size of the parameter class. We introduce a novel upper bound for regret in contextual linear bandits that adapts to the distribution's knowledge, and we derive a lower bound for contextual bandits with specific context distributions. Our results show that if the context distribution is known and the parameter class is sparse, then the required communication bits can be significantly reduced.

The prevailing approach to addressing class imbalance in predictive models involves methods that intentionally bias the data distribution to favor the minority class. Conversely, we propose an alternative strategy, where oversampling the majority class to the point of class imbalance reversal, thereby inverting the effects of class imbalance. In essence, this approach reverses the decision boundary to better represent the minority class. In our study, we tested this novel method using a range of oversampling techniques on 12 datasets and compared its performance to existing methods. The results demonstrate that our approach outperforms current solutions, with notable success in both balanced and imbalanced accuracy.

The LHCb experiment has conducted an in-depth analysis of the $D^+\to
K^{*+}\epsilon_+$ decay, utilizing a substantial dataset of 3 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collision data, to determine the complex ratio of two key components in this process. This study is crucial for enhancing the precision of future measurements related to the $W\) mass, the $U$-triangle angle, and the $D$ meson charm-mixing parameters and the violation of $C$-parity in charm particles.

A recent investigation into the reproducibility of research has highlighted the significant impact of statistical methods and sample size on study outcomes, leading to a call for the standardization of statistical reporting to facilitate the verification of published results. In response, we propose that a similar approach can be applied to confirm published research claims in fields outside of experimental sciences. By utilizing existing bibliometric metrics, researchers can replicate key aspects of published research, such as data collection, to verify original findings. We demonstrate the utility of these metrics by applying them to confirm recent findings on the impact of social media on the spread of information during the COVID-19 pandemic.

A groundbreaking technique known as 'flying focus X' has been developed to control
the spatial and temporal characteristics of a laser beam by rapidly moving it
in-time and space. This innovative approach, which can be achieved using a single
electromagnetic coil, offers unparalleled flexibility and efficiency in
applying laser-based methods. Its versatility allows it to be used in various
scenarios, including the generation of high-intensity femtosecond pulses, and it
can be easily integrated into existing laser systems.

The FIRA HuroCup league has been driving advancements in humanoid robots for over 15 years, pushing the boundaries of robotic design and AI through its annual competitions. Since 2005, the HuroCup league has required participants to navigate a challenging obstacle course in a timed challenge, modeled after the South Korean sport, Taekkoni. To develop more sophisticated robots, the HuroCup league has long incorporated simulation environments and automated challenge generators. However, the HuroCup simulation has previously lacked a comprehensive, open-source implementation, such as PyBullet, which this research aims to address. Our PyHuroCup implementation integrates the HuroCup challenge generator, simulation, and robot controller in a unified Python-based framework, leveraging PyBullet's capabilities and providing a detailed analysis of its design and evaluation through a series of simulation tests.

Cross-domain recommendation has been a highly researched area in the field of recommendation systems. However, the current methods mainly rely on aligning similar user-item pairs across different domains through either semantic features or attention-based techniques. In contrast, this study proposes a novel approach that leverages metric learning to learn the distance between user-item pairs in a unified space. By employing metric learning, the proposed method can effectively capture the nuanced differences in user-item behavior across various domains. Furthermore, the incorporation of a contrastive loss can enhance the cross-domain alignment by minimizing the distance between similar pairs and maximizing the distance between dissimilar pairs. Experimental results on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method over existing approaches.

This paper presents a novel automaton model, specifically designed to analyze systems with asynchronous and asynchronous communication between finite-state machines, where the former uses external memory and the latter use internal memory, leading to distinct transition and acceptance languages. We investigate the expressive power of these automata, establish relationships with asynchronous automata models, demonstrate the equivalence to a modified version of asynchronous automata, and show that they can replicate the acceptance language of asynchronous tree-walking automata over ordered trees.

A new model has been developed to study heat transfer within two-dimensional plasma layers. Based on experimental observations, this model incorporates the effects of both thermal ions and a fixed, equilibrium background of electrons. It uses a vibrational approach to account for the complex plasma's internal energy and employs the Boltzmann transport model to describe the fluid dynamics. The model has been reduced to a single, nonlinear partial differential equation, which has been solved using a Maple software implementation. The resulting solution, expressed in terms of the extended hypergeometric function, has been shown to be applicable across a broad range of physical parameters. When applied to the specific context of two-dimensional plasma, this solution yields results that align well with existing theoretical predictions and experimental measurements.

This study explores the connection between two systems, counter machines with unordered data and coloured Petri nets, by establishing a correspondence between them. Our analysis reveals that any problem that can be solved by a counter machine with unordered data can also be solved by a coloured Petri net. Additionally, we found that these two systems are equivalent in their ability to describe the properties of data streams. This research contributes to the field of language recognition and provides a new tool for translating problems into the language recognition framework.

The current high frame rate coronary angiography (HFCAs) technology is capable of capturing high-speed video, but it lacks sufficient resolution. To address this limitation, a new approach is proposed that uses a deep learning network to generate high-resolution HFCAs videos from lower-resolution ones. The network, composed of a U-Net and a convolutional neural network, is designed to produce high-resolution frames from lower-resolution input frames. The network is trained on a large dataset of HFCAs videos and is then fine-tuned using a temporal and spatial consistency loss function. The results show that this method can effectively improve the signal-to-noise ratio of HFCAs videos, with peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) values increasing by 2.42 dB and structural similarity index (SSIM) values improving by 0.14. The proposed method outperforms traditional interpolation techniques, such as Bicubic and Motion Bicubic, in terms of PSNR and SSIM values. The high-speed videos synthesized using this method demonstrate superior visual effects compared to existing methods.

The exceptionally clean environment of FCC-ee allows for precise searches for rare particle decays that are challenging to detect due to the presence of background noise from standard particle decays and cosmic rays. Thanks to the superior detector capabilities and the vast amount of data available, scientists at FCC-ee have the opportunity to make groundbreaking discoveries in this field. In this paper, we examine the potential for identifying rare processes in the decays of heavy particles such as the $B_s^0$, $K^{*+}$, and $K_{S,L}^0$, and we assess the feasibility of detecting these processes using the proposed FCC detectors.

We investigate the potential of using coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering to enhance dark matter direct detection experiments. By leveraging the neutrino-related improvements in CE$\nu$NS, we can measure the nuclear response function associated with this process, which is then connected to the electron-induced nuclear response function. This relationship allows us to improve dark matter direct detection experiments by incorporating the electron-induced nuclear response function. We find that significant improvements in Dark Matter Direct Detection experiments can be made using this approach, with the enhancement being dependent on the electron-induced nuclear response function and the specific characteristics of the DM particle.

The gravitational influence of an intermediate-mass companion on a binary star system can cause the stars to orbit the black hole differently, leading to a variety of orbital paths around the time a star is consumed. This results in a range of possible orbits for the second star before it eventually falls into the black hole. By examining the effects of this process, we have determined a range of possible times for a second star to fall into the black hole after a first star has been caught by the intermediate-mass companion. This can occur across a range of orbital periods and masses around a $10^6$ solar mass black hole.

This research explores the solution to a stochastic differential equation that has been significantly disturbed by fractional Brownian motion. The key characteristics of the solution, specifically its continuity, the distribution of its magnitude, the distribution of its maximum value, and the distribution of its time spent away from predetermined sets, are investigated. The primary findings indicate that these characteristics are heavily influenced by the HURST PARAMETER and the scale of the disturbance. The results are derived from the analysis of the solutions to a specific class of SDEs that have been perturbed by fractional Brownian motion. The obtained results are then applied to a specific SDE, which models the movement of a particle influenced by a magnetic field. The solution to this SDE is a combination of two different processes, specifically the fractional Brownian motion and the Brownian motion, which are used to derive the distribution of its magnitude, its maximum value, and the distribution of its time spent away from a specific set.

We demonstrate that for every $1 \leq K \leq \text{cons}(ZFC, c)$, there exists a nonstationary ideal $\mathcal I_K$ on $\omega_1$ that can be defined using a $\Sigma_1$ formula with a set parameter, where $K$ is of size $K$. Furthermore, for every $1 \leq K \leq \text{cons}(ZFC, c)$, it can be proven that there exists a family $\mathcal F_K$ of $K$ many perfect k-path hash functions from $\omega$ to $\omega$, where the family $\mathcal F_K$ is closed under finite rearrangements, such that for every $\varphi \in \text{L}(\omega, \omega)$, the set of all $\varphi$-indexed functions in $\mathcal F_K$ is not $\varphi$-equivalent to any ideal $\mathcal I_K$-selective function.

Multitask training is a key strategy for enhancing the performance of single-task models, yet pinpointing the most effective task combinations for this approach remains a challenge. This paper proposes a novel framework for multitask training, dubbed M2T, which streamlines the model training and evaluation process through automation. M2T is integrated into the PyTorch library and can be accessed via the `torch.mlt` module. The paper showcases the benefits of M2T through a series of experiments, which demonstrate the potential for improved performance on various downstream tasks, as well as the capacity for rapid model training and evaluation. Additionally, the paper highlights the importance of thorough experimentation in the context of multitask learning and emphasizes the practical advantages of the M2T framework.

The development of large-scale traffic sign datasets has been instrumental in driving the success of machine learning algorithms for traffic sign detection. Although these datasets have primarily been used for fine-tuning classifiers, the underlying traffic sign bounding boxes in these datasets have not been utilised to improve object detection models. This paper presents a novel approach to leveraging traffic sign bounding boxes in a dataset, specifically through the annotation of non-sign objects in images, resulting in a significant dataset of over 1.5 million annotated traffic signs and non-sign objects. This dataset has been demonstrated to yield substantial improvements in deep convolutional neural network (CNN) detectors when used for transfer learning. Notably, the use of this dataset has resulted in a significant 10% improvement in the KITTI traffic sign detection metric when fine-tuning a Faster R-CNN detector, and up to a 30% improvement in the mAP for the DPM detector.

Recommending personalized items is a complex task that has been extensively researched in the field of data mining.  Traditional methods rely on collecting user feedback data, which is often time-consuming and expensive.  To address this challenge, we introduce SelfCF, a novel framework that enables personalized recommendations without relying on explicit user feedback training data.  Leveraging the principles of self-supervised learning, SelfCF employs a dual contrastive learning approach to learn high-quality item representations and develop effective recommendation models.  By incorporating a unique loss function, SelfCF can effectively identify and learn the patterns in the recommendation matrix, achieving state-of-the-art recommendation accuracy while significantly reducing training time compared to conventional methods.  Comprehensive experiments conducted on multiple datasets demonstrate the efficacy of SelfCF in delivering accurate recommendations up to 100x faster than its supervised counterparts.

In this research, we're examining how to count smooth projective covers of specific curves, with a particular emphasis on their singularities. We're interested in how extra rules for where the cover's singularities occur affect the count, with a focus on how these additional rules interact. Specifically, we've developed a new approach to solving this problem, by breaking it down into simpler cases, and then using this approach to reprove an existing solution to a related problem, while also gaining additional insights in the process.

In a gapped Dirac semimetal, high-energy excitations exhibit unique characteristics, characterized by the "flat band" and "Weyl bands." The density of states and optical conductivity in this high-energy range are significantly influenced by the accumulation of states at the edges of the gapped energy band, resulting in distinct features. Specifically, the density of states displays a peak, while the optical conductivity is reduced in comparison to the semimetallic state, which is a characteristic of the gapped Dirac semimetal.

In the context of population dynamics, we examine a differential system that exhibits periodic coefficients, and investigate its limit behavior in the case of an infinitely long period. Utilizing the concept of slow variables, we demonstrate that this system can be transformed into a singular perturbation problem. However, our analysis reveals that the conventional method of perturbation of levels is insufficient for distinguishing between fast and slow variables, particularly when the period is significantly longer than the period of oscillations. To address this issue, we develop an alternative approach that identifies the slow variables as the largest ones, and proves the existence of a slow and exponential stable manifold associated with the system's slow-fast flow.

We have developed a method to calculate the gravitational wave signal of binary black hole mergers using high-precision numerical relativity simulations. By applying a spectral approach, we can model the waveforms of black hole binaries with different masses and spins, and then use them to predict the detection rates of specific gravitational wave modes in future space-based observatories. Our results indicate that third-generation detectors will be able to detect around 190 events with certain gravitational wave patterns, while a hypothetical fourth-generation detector could detect over 1,000 binary mergers. Additionally, we found that detectors with higher precision will be able to detect rare gravitational wave patterns, such as the (3,3) and (4,4) modes, which will occur at least 0.5-1.5 times per year.

A recently developed astrometric method allows for the identification of binary systems containing a black hole, based on the characteristics of the orbiting partner. This method utilizes the orbital parameters of the companion star to predict its position relative to a reference point, and compares it to actual observations made by the \emph{Hubble Space Telescope}. The method is effective for detecting astrometric binaries with black hole companions in the M-type systems, and can be applied to various M-type systems with different orbital distances. The method is also being developed to be applied to other types of binary systems that contain black holes, and can be used to determine the mass of the black hole through a comparison of the predicted and observed astrometric positions.

This study examines the convergence rate of the $(1 + 1)$ evolutionary algorithm for the 0/1 knapsack problem. By applying the Hamiltonian dynamics framework, we derive the mean-square convergence rate of the population variance. Our analysis reveals that the combination of uniform crossover and tournament selection achieves the maximum convergence rate. Our theoretical findings are supported by experimental results, which demonstrate the superiority of this selection scheme combination.

This paper focuses on L^2 estimates for oscillatory integrals with specific conditions: either smooth or polynomial phases, and with no more than third-degree derivatives. It is found that L^2 estimates behave differently for oscillatory integrals with smooth phases compared to those with polynomial phases. We derive a L^2 estimate for oscillatory integrals with smooth phases on finite energy manifolds, a result that cannot be achieved for oscillatory integrals with polynomial phases. This new estimate is crucial for analyzing the global behavior of the wave equation on asymptotically hyperbolic Einstein-Minkowski spaces with Cauchy-Hadamard singularities.
